summary: Reports on the IAB workshop on Measuring Network Quality for End-Users, held virtually on 14 to 16 September 2021. It summarizes the topics discussed and the preliminary conclusions drawn. It reflects the views of workshop participants rather than the IAB. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Experts met online to talk about how to tell whether your Internet is good, beyond just speed. This is the write-up of what they said.

questions: how to measure network quality for end users
what was the iab network quality workshop
what makes good internet quality beyond speed
why is latency important for user experience
what metrics matter most for internet connections
subtitle: What makes a good Internet connection beyond just speed.

tldr.problem: The networking industry has focused on throughput (bandwidth) as the primary metric of Internet quality, but this metric alone does not correlate well with user experience. End users often suffer from high latency, unreliable connectivity, and poor application responsiveness despite having high bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: An IAB workshop in September 2021 gathered experts to discuss what metrics actually matter for end-user experience, including latency, availability, reliability, and application responsiveness.
tldr.outcome: The workshop produced consensus statements about the importance of measuring metrics beyond bandwidth, the need for continuous passive measurements, and the requirement that metrics be actionable for networks and applications.

today: RFC 9318 is an Informational document published in October 2022 reporting the outcomes of the IAB workshop. It remains current as guidance for network measurement and quality assessment initiatives.

sections.title: Beyond Throughput: The Problem with Speed-Only Metrics
sections.content:
This RFC documents a workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) in September 2021 to address a fundamental problem: the Internet industry has narrowly focused on throughput (bandwidth) as the primary measure of Internet quality, but users' actual quality of experience depends on many other factors.

Even with gigabit connections available in many places, users experience poor performance due to high latency, packet loss, and service interruptions. End-user latency has not significantly improved in a decade, despite remarkable advances in available bandwidth. Additionally, because consumers are offered mostly high-throughput devices, the perception that higher throughput always means better service has become entrenched, even when the real problems are latency and reliability.

Applications have developed various techniques to hide latency effects (such as caching), further decoupling user experience from network metrics. The workshop aimed to identify metrics that actually predict good user experience and are actionable for networks and applications to improve.
sections.eli5: We have fast Internet but it still feels slow sometimes. The industry focused on speed (bandwidth) but forgot about responsiveness (latency) and reliability. This workshop asked: what really matters to users?

sections.title: Key Metrics and Measurement Approaches
sections.content:
The workshop identified several important metrics beyond throughput. Availability measures whether users have connectivity at all. Capacity measures the maximum data rate a path can carry, important for video streaming and file downloads. Latency measures the delay of individual packets, affecting interactive applications like videoconferencing and gaming.

The workshop distinguished between active measurements (where a user deliberately sends test traffic) and passive measurements (where actual application traffic is observed). Both are needed: active measurements provide controlled testing, while passive measurements capture real-world performance and enable historical analysis for debugging.

A key finding was that Round-trips Per Minute (RPM) — how many request-response cycles an application can complete in a minute — is a meaningful metric that users can understand. The workshop also noted that latency distribution (understanding the tail latency) matters more than average latency for user experience.
sections.eli5: Can you reach the Internet? How much data at once? How fast do responses come back? These matter more than just top speed. Real-world measurements from your apps matter more than speed tests.

sections.title: Cross-Layer Considerations and Protocol Evolution
sections.content:
The workshop emphasized that performance depends on interactions across multiple layers of the network stack. The oldest queuing algorithms in home routers still use simple FIFO (First In, First Out) queuing, which causes high latency when routers are busy. Recent advances in algorithm design (like CoDel) can reduce latency under load, but many routers have not adopted these improvements due to cost and marketing pressures. System-on-Chip manufacturers prioritize throughput acceleration, assuming consumers want raw speed.

The workshop discussed how new transport protocols like QUIC are evolving more rapidly than older kernel-resident protocols like TCP, offering better latency properties. However, backward compatibility concerns have slowed adoption of improvements: the IPv6 transition has taken 25+ years with incomplete deployment, demonstrating how difficult it is to change fundamental Internet infrastructure.

The workshop also noted that improvements in one area (higher bandwidth) can paradoxically worsen latency perception if overselling leads to queuing delays. Users may genuinely need latency improvements, not bandwidth upgrades, but the industry's focus on throughput marketing means they receive bandwidth upgrades instead.
sections.eli5: Routers are still using old ways of managing traffic that cause delays. Different parts of the network (apps, routers, protocols) need to work together better. Switching to better technology takes forever because of backward compatibility.

sections.title: Actionable Metrics and Stakeholder Alignment
sections.content:
A crucial conclusion from the workshop is that metrics must be actionable — they should provide incentive for improvements. A good metric should help networks identify problems, enable application developers to optimize for user experience, and allow users to choose better service providers.

Research by regulators shows that end users prefer simple, categorical choices such as "good", "better", and "best" rather than detailed technical metrics. Users want to know whether their application will work properly or fail, not complex statistics about their network.

However, stakeholder incentives are not aligned. The networking industry benefits from selling more bandwidth, while users need latency improvements. Application vendors develop proprietary "secret sauce" metrics that do not generalize. To drive improvements, measurements need to be shared, standardized, and made visible to all stakeholders.

The workshop noted that new measurement techniques should not rely solely on reading TCP headers (which encryption increasingly prevents). Instead, measurements should work across different protocol types and respect privacy concerns.
sections.eli5: Metrics need to make companies want to get better. Simple answers matter to users (does it work?), not expert-level details. But companies have different goals: providers want to sell speed, apps want their "secret recipe". Everyone needs to agree on what matters.

sections.title: Future Directions and Follow-On Work
sections.content:
The workshop identified several areas needing further work. Some improvements can happen in existing IETF working groups (IPPM for measurements, DetNet for deterministic networks, RAW for reliability), while longer-term research is needed through IRTF groups.

A lower-latency Internet would benefit all end users, but incontrovertible evidence of which metric (latency vs. speed) is more important has not yet persuaded device vendors to prioritize latency optimization. The workshop also raised emerging concerns like the ecological impact of material and energy usage in networking infrastructure.

The workshop emphasized that measurement without improvement is frustrating. The goal is not just to document poor performance but to use measurements as a tool to drive competitive market incentives and industry practices toward better user experience. Success requires alignment of incentives across ISPs, equipment vendors, application developers, and end users.
sections.eli5: There is still work to do. Experts need to build tools that measure the right things. Companies need reasons to care about latency as much as speed. Measuring is only useful if it leads to getting better.
